cur:objects-bm-deesis-ivory.summary: Beneath a pierced arcade Christ stands frontally on a footstool, holding a book and blessing; the Virgin at the left and St John the Baptist at the right lift their hands toward him in intercession. The tall, finely draped figures stand in a shallow space, isolated against the plain ivory ground. The plaque is a compact image of the Church's prayer before Christ.
facts: The British Museum dates the plaque to about 900–1000 (registration number 1923,1205.2) and displays it in Room 40.

Q116242906.summary: Pressed into a small disc of dark glass, this balance weight bears worn busts: a central figure above, identified by the Metropolitan Museum as Christ blessing, and two figures below, officials (eparchs) or emperors. Such glass weights, stamped by the authorities, guaranteed honest measure in the marketplace, and Christ's image placed that guarantee under divine sanction.
facts: The weight is only about 2 cm across and weighs 2 grams.
Byzantine glass weights were often stamped with the names or images of the eparch (city prefect) responsible for supervising weights and measures.
Q116242906.notes: The moulded image is heavily worn; the three busts are visible, but identification of the upper figure as Christ relies on the Met's catalogue. No scripture passage applies directly (Proverbs 11:1 on just weights could be cited as theme).

wga:zearly/1/2mural/3priscil/1greek8.summary: On the arch of the Greek Chapel (Cappella Greca), three Magi in short tunics stride in single file toward a seated figure at the right, the Virgin, who once held the Christ Child on her lap. The figures are painted in quick, warm strokes against the pale plaster, and though the Child is now hard to make out, the scene is one of the earliest representations of the Gentiles coming to worship the newborn King.
facts: The Greek Chapel takes its name from two Greek inscriptions painted in a niche; it contains 3rd-century frescoes of Old and New Testament scenes, including the famous 'Fractio Panis'.
In early Christian art the Magi are typically shown, as here, in short tunics striding toward the seated Mother and Child, a formula repeated on many 4th-century sarcophagi.
wga:zearly/1/2mural/3priscil/1greek8.notes: The Christ Child is not clearly legible in the photograph because of the fresco's condition; the identification rests on the established reading of the scene.
